claims.evidence: This is specific architectural information from the BERT paper.

claims.claim: BERTLARGE results surpassed BERTBASE results on all tasks, indicating the importance of model size for performance.
claims.source: The authors found that the BERTLARGE results surpassed the results of BERTBASE on all the tasks, which indicates the importance of the model size for the performance.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the BERT paper.

claims.claim: There has been increased interest in Transformer models for applications in computational biology and bioinformatics due to recent successes in NLP tasks.
claims.source: Because of the recent successes of DL-based language models in a myriad of NLP tasks, and particularly so when using the Transformer model, there has been an increased interest in such models for applications in other fields, such as in computational biology and bioinformatics.
claims.evidence: This is an observation about trends in the field.

claims.claim: NLP models can be applied to sequences of genomic or proteomic data, and recent results indicate this is a highly successful approach for protein prediction applications.
claims.source: In these fields, NLP models can be applied to sequences of, for example, genomic or proteomic data, and recent results indicate that this is a highly successful approach for protein prediction applications (Choromanski et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Choromanski et al., 2020.

claims.claim: DL models are known to be computationally expensive and take considerable time to train.
claims.source: DL models are known to be computationally expensive and to take considerable amount of time to train.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about DL models.

claims.claim: Transformer models avoid some challenges associated with traditional DL methods for sequence modeling.
claims.source: The Transformer models, however, avoid some of the challenges associated with traditional DL methods for sequence modelling.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the subsequent discussion of specific advantages.

claims.claim: RNN models suffer from vanishing and exploding gradient problems, making them difficult to train.
claims.source: But in doing so, they do not capture any input sequence context from the other side of the current position in the sequence. They also suffer from some fundamental problems (called the vanishing and exploding gradient problems) (Bengio et al., 1994; Pascanu et al., 2013; Hanin, 2018), which makes them difficult to train (Dai et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Bengio et al., 1994, Pascanu et al., 2013, Hanin, 2018, and Dai et al., 2018.

claims.claim: RNN models have problems learning relationships between distant tokens in an input sequence.
claims.source: The effect of this is that RNN models have problems to learn relationships between distant tokens in an input sequence (Bengio et al., 1994; Pascanu et al., 2013; Hanin, 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Bengio et al., 1994, Pascanu et al., 2013, and Hanin, 2018.

claims.claim: RNN training is slow because data is processed one token at a time and computations cannot be parallelized.
claims.source: Also, since the data is processed one token at a time, it is not possible to parallelize the computations, making the training slow (Wang et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2019.

claims.claim: For CNNs to capture distant features in input, they need to learn a hierarchy of features, which may require many levels and can make CNNs slow.
claims.source: For a CNN to capture distant features in the input, they need to learn a hierarchy of features. It may take many such hierarchy levels to extract meaningful information from a larger part of an input sequence (Raghu et al., 2021), which can make CNNs slow.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Raghu et al., 2021.

claims.claim: CNNs are invariant to spatial translations and do not utilize positional information that may be relevant in an input sequence.
claims.source: CNNs are also invariant to spatial translations and do therefore not utilize the positional information that may be relevant in an input sequence (Albawi et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Albawi et al., 2017.

claims.claim: While CNNs have had remarkable success on image data, they have not been as successful in sequence modeling.
claims.source: While CNNs have had a remarkable success on, for example., image data, they have not been as successful in sequence modelling.
claims.evidence: This is an observation based on established knowledge in the field.

claims.claim: The Transformer model's attention module allows each token to influence weights for every other token in the sequence, enabling it to attend to long-range dependencies.
claims.source: The Transformer model's attention module allows each token to influence weights for every other token in the sequence. This allows the Transformer model to attend to long-range dependencies between input tokens, a very beneficial property since it enables Transformers to consider the whole context of an input sequence (Dehghani et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Dehghani et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Transformers obtain superior results and sequence embeddings compared to other models.
claims.source: As a result, they obtain superior results and sequence embeddings (Väth et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Väth et al., 2022.

claims.claim: Direct connections between distant tokens in Transformers help when training the models, making them easy to train.
claims.source: The direct connections between distant tokens also help when training the Transformer models, making it easy to train them (Dai et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Dai et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Transformer models are highly parallelizable and have simple components, making them computationally attractive.
claims.source: The Transformer models are also highly parallelizable, and only have simple components such as attention modules and fully connected layers, which makes them computationally attractive (Wang et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Models used in NLP can be used to learn and understand protein sequences and are commonly referred to as protein language models.
claims.source: The models used in the field of NLP can thus also be used to learn and understand protein sequences and in this context, they are commonly referred to as protein language models (Heinzinger et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Heinzinger et al., 2019.

claims.claim: While there are abstract similarities between sentences and protein sequences, there are major differences in their properties, syntax, and semantics.
claims.source: While there are abstract similarities between sentences and protein sequences, there are of course major differences in their properties, syntax, and semantics (Ofer et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Ofer et al., 2021.

claims.claim: When handling proteins, a word can be one of the twenty canonical amino acids or a group of amino acids, while a protein sequence corresponds to a sentence.
claims.source: When handling proteins, a word can be one of the individual twenty canonical amino acids (excluding unconventional and rare amino acids) Lopez and Mohiuddin, 2020 found in the genetic code or it could be a number of these amino acids grouped together, while a protein sequence would correspond to a sentence (Ferruz et al., 2022; ElAbd et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Lopez and Mohiuddin, 2020, Ferruz et al., 2022, and ElAbd et al., 2020.

claims.claim: Individual amino acids as words is the most common approach in protein language models.
claims.source: A word being individual amino acids is the most common approach, and other alternatives do not appear to have been explored much (Ofer et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Ofer et al., 2021.

claims.claim: Protein sequences contain long-range dependencies, making them excellent candidates for analysis by Transformers.
claims.source: Just like with natural language, protein sequences contain long-range dependencies, making them excellent candidates for analysis by recent NLP models such as Transformers (Ofer et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Ofer et al., 2021.

claims.claim: The largest open sources of protein sequence information are UniProt, Pfam, and the Big Fantastic Database (BFD).
claims.source: The largest open sources of protein sequence information and data are the Universal Protein Resource (UniProt) (UniProt, 2021), Pfam (Mistry et al., 2021), and the Big Fantastic Database (BFD) (BFD, 2022).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to UniProt, 2021, Mistry et al., 2021, and BFD, 2022.

claims.claim: UniProt contains around 0.567M reviewed and manually annotated sequences and more than 230M automatically annotated sequences.
claims.source: UniProt contains around 0.567M sequences that are reviewed and manually annotated and more than 230M sequences that are automatically annotated.
claims.evidence: This is specific data about UniProt.

claims.claim: Pfam is a database containing protein families determined by similar functional domains.
claims.source: The Pfam is a database containing protein families, where a family is determined by similar functional domains.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about Pfam.

claims.claim: Pfam currently has 19,632 families and clans and contains 61M sequences as per Pfam 35.0.
claims.source: Pfam currently has 19,632 families and clans (higher-level groupings), as per Pfam 35.0, and contains a total of 61M sequences (Pfam 35.0, 2021).
claims.evidence: This is specific data about Pfam supported by citation.

claims.claim: BFD comprises 65.9M families covering more than 2B protein sequences and was built using UniProt and a reference protein catalogue clustered to 30% sequence identity.
claims.source: BFD is a very large collection of protein families publicly available. It comprises 65.9M families covering more than 2B protein sequences and was built using UniProt, and a reference protein catalogue (Steinegger et al., 2019), clustered to 30% sequence identity.
claims.evidence: This is specific data about BFD supported by citation to Steinegger et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Protein language models are typically trained on large open collections of protein data.
claims.source: Protein language models are typically trained on such large open collections of protein data.
claims.evidence: This is established practice in the field.

claims.claim: Using self-supervised training on large databases of proteins, protein language models can learn very complex relationships and patterns in protein sequences through the global biome and across time.
claims.source: Using self-supervised training procedures on large databases of proteins, protein language models are able to learn very complex relationships and patterns in protein sequences through the global biome and across time.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on how these models work.

claims.claim: Large protein language models are used for downstream applications using either feature-based or fine-tuning approaches.
claims.source: Large protein language models, trained using one of the two approaches described above (Figure 3B) on very large databases of protein sequences, are used for downstream applications using one of two common approaches (Laskar et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Laskar et al., 2020.

claims.claim: In the feature-based approach, a model is trained in a self-supervised manner and the trained model's representation is used as a feature vector for downstream tasks.
claims.source: The first, called feature-based, is where a model is trained in a self-supervised manner, for instance, using one of the two approaches illustrated in Figure 3B, without any labels. The trained model's representation of each protein sequence is then considered a feature vector for a protein that can directly be used for downstream protein prediction tasks.
claims.evidence: This is a description of a standard approach in the field.

claims.claim: In the fine-tuning approach, a model is first trained in a self-supervised manner and then updated using protein sequences with labels of interest.
claims.source: The second, called fine-tuning, is where a model is trained first in a self-supervised manner without any labels for the protein sequences, and then updated, or fine-tuned, using protein sequences with labels of interest.
claims.evidence: This is a description of a standard approach in the field.

claims.claim: Protein prediction tasks for which the Transformer has been used include predictions of protein structure, protein residue contact, protein-protein interactions, drug-target interactions, PTMs, and homology studies.
claims.source: Protein prediction tasks for which the Transformer has been used include predictions of protein structure, protein residue contact, protein–protein interactions (PPI), drug–target interactions (DTI), PTMs, and homology studies.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of applications discussed in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The fixed size Transformer representation for local tasks can be obtained by taking a fixed window around sites of interest.
claims.source: The fixed size Transformer representation for the local task can be obtained by taking a fixed window around the sites of interest, while the fixed size representation of a protein for a global task is achieved, for instance, by averaging the residue vectors to yield the protein sequence vector (Väth et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Väth et al., 2022.

claims.claim: Most state-of-the-art techniques for protein predictions have been based on features from profile-to-profile comparison created from multiple sequence alignments using tools such as PSI-BLAST and HMMER.
claims.source: Most of the state-of-the-art techniques for such predictions have been based on features from profile-to-profile comparison created from multiple sequence alignments (MSAs) of proteins using tools such as PSI-BLAST (Altschul et al., 1997) and HMMER (Finn et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Altschul et al., 1997 and Finn et al., 2011.

claims.claim: MSA-based techniques have limitations due to gaps in protein sequences from deletions and insertions.
claims.source: However, such techniques have limitations due to the existence of gaps in the protein sequences stemming from deletions and insertions (Golubchik et al., 2007) and work unsatisfactory for sequences having few to no homologs to generate MSA and profiles (Phuong et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Golubchik et al., 2007 and Phuong et al., 2006.

claims.claim: Predicted structural features suffer a limitation since the structural information problem is yet to be solved, resulting in imperfect features.
claims.source: Moreover, predicted structural features, such as secondary structure, have also been popular when developing predictive models, but they suffer a limitation since the structural information problem is yet to be solved, which results in imperfect features (Sułkowska et al., 2012; Schmiedel and Lehner, 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Sułkowska et al., 2012 and Schmiedel and Lehner, 2019.

claims.claim: Results obtained using Transformer models on protein prediction tasks have been quite promising without the use of MSA tools or structural information.
claims.source: The results obtained using Transformer models on such tasks have been quite promising, and without the use of MSA tools that require homologous sequences, and also without structural information.
claims.evidence: This is a summary observation based on the review of multiple studies.

claims.claim: A Transformer-based framework by Chowdhury et al., 2022 outperformed AlphaFold2 in structure prediction for sequences that lack homologs.
claims.source: A recent framework introduced by Chowdhury et al., 2022, which has a Transformer-based language model at its core, outperformed AlphaFold2 (Jumper et al., 2021), an MSA-based approach, in structure prediction for sequences that lack homologs.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Chowdhury et al., 2022 and Jumper et al., 2021.

claims.claim: MSA tools generate alignment by searching homologs from the entire UniProt database, which is a time-consuming process.
claims.source: MSA tools generate alignment by searching homologs from the entire UniProt database, time-consuming (Hong et al., 2021) process, whereby generating embeddings using protein language models is less cumbersome but it also builds richer and more complete features for low homologous proteins (Wang et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Hong et al., 2021 and Wang et al., 2022.

claims.claim: Generating embeddings using protein language models is less cumbersome and builds richer features for low homologous proteins compared to MSA tools.
claims.source: MSA tools generate alignment by searching homologs from the entire UniProt database, time-consuming (Hong et al., 2021) process, whereby generating embeddings using protein language models is less cumbersome but it also builds richer and more complete features for low homologous proteins (Wang et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2022.

claims.claim: A protein's structure is encoded in its amino acid composition, and both composition and structure can determine a protein's function.
claims.source: The structure is encoded in a protein's amino acid composition, and both the composition and the structure can determine a protein's function (Jumper et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Jumper et al., 2021 and is established knowledge.

claims.claim: Protein structure prediction can be broken down into secondary structure (α-helix, β-sheet, or coil) and tertiary structure (3D shape).
claims.source: The protein structure prediction task can be broken down into two categories: secondary structure (α-helix, β-sheet, or coil) and tertiary structure (3D shape).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about protein structure.

claims.claim: Protein contact prediction can be formulated as binary classification, multiclass classification, or regression.
claims.source: Protein contact prediction can be formulated as either a binary classification problem (whether two residues have a close distance between their central carbon atoms), a multiclass classification problem (encapsulating real distance predictions by dividing the distance measurements into discrete bins), or as a regression problem (predicting real-valued distances).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about how contact prediction is approached.

claims.claim: Rives et al., 2021 predicted secondary structure and contact by training a neural network classifier using sequence profile features combined with ESM-1b Transformer representation, showing improved performance on the CASP test set.
claims.source: For example, Rives et al., 2021 predicted secondary structure and contact by training a neural network classifier using sequence profile features combined with the representation from their ESM-1b Transformer model. They evaluated the feature combination on the Critical Assessment of protein Structure Prediction (CASP) test set (Kryshtafovych et al., 2019), and the results show an improved performance compared with other models.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Rives et al., 2021 and Kryshtafovych et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Singh et al., 2022 showed improvements over evolutionary-profile-based methods for contact prediction using ESM-1b features combined with one-hot encoding and SPOT-1D-Single.
claims.source: Other works on contact predictions include utilizing the feature combination of one-hot encoding, SPOT-1D-Single (Singh et al., 2021), and the representation from ESM-1b (Rives et al., 2021) to train a neural network classifier. This showed improvements over evolutionary-profile-based methods and over using ESM-1b representation alone (Singh et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Singh et al., 2021, Rives et al., 2021, and Singh et al., 2022.

claims.claim: Zhang et al., 2021 pre-trained a novel Transformer that outperformed the winner group of CASP14 contact prediction challenge on the CASP14 benchmark.
claims.source: Moreover, a novel Transformer was pre-trained and utilized the CASP14 benchmark (Kryshtafovych et al., 2019) for contact prediction that outperformed the winner group of CASP14 contact prediction challenge (Zhang et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Kryshtafovych et al., 2019 and Zhang et al., 2021.

claims.claim: In homology prediction, a non-annotated protein with unknown biological function is characterized by finding evolutionary related sequences with known function.
claims.source: In homology prediction, a non-annotated protein with unknown biological function is characterized by finding evolutionary related sequences with known function (Gromiha et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Gromiha et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Detection of remote homologs is of great interest in microbiology and medicine, for instance to detect emerging antibiotic-resistant genes.
claims.source: In microbiology and medicine, detection of remote homologs is of great interest, for instance, to detect emerging antibiotic-resistant genes (Tavares et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Tavares et al., 2013.

claims.claim: A major issue with MSA-based tools is that they fail to determine sequences that are distantly related (remote homology).
claims.source: A major issue with these tools is that they fail to determine sequences that are distantly related (remote homology) (Wilburn and Eddy, 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Wilburn and Eddy, 2020.

claims.claim: Zare-Mirakabad et al., 2021 utilized ProtAlbert to predict a protein's profile and concluded that high similarity between predicted and HSSP database profiles indicates the usefulness of their approach.
claims.source: A new method was introduced by Zare-Mirakabad et al., 2021 that utilizes a pre-trained Transformer called ProtAlbert (Elnaggar et al., 2020b) to predict a protein's profile. To predict the profile for a protein, the protein sequence with masked tokens was fed to the model and predicted the most likely amino acids in those masked positions. The predicted profiles were compared with the sequence profiles in the HSSP dataset (Dodge et al., 1998). They concluded that the high similarity between the two profiles (predicted and HSSP database) indicates the usefulness of their approach, and that it can assist researchers in obtaining prediction profiles for new sequences.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Zare-Mirakabad et al., 2021, Elnaggar et al., 2020b, and Dodge et al., 1998.

claims.claim: Heinzinger et al., 2022 used contrastive learning with ProtT5 embeddings for homology detection and found it required less pre-processing time than HMMER profiles and showed similar or better performance.
claims.source: Contrastive learning, which involves finding an embedding space where similar samples are brought together while dissimilar ones pushed apart, was investigated by Heinzinger et al., 2022. The work utilized embeddings from the ProtT5 (Elnaggar et al., 2020a) pre-trained Transformer model that were mapped using a feed-forward neural network to a new embedding space. The similarity between pairs, using Euclidean distance in the embedding space, was used to find homologous sequences, as well as to identify more distant relations. They observed that this approach required significantly less protein pre-processing time compared to MSA profiles from tools such as HMMER (Finn et al., 2011). Their results not only showed similar performance to HMMER (Finn et al., 2011) profiles but outperformed it for distant relations.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Heinzinger et al., 2022, Elnaggar et al., 2020a, and Finn et al., 2011.

claims.claim: Behjati et al., 2022 found that attention heads of the pre-trained ProtAlbert Transformer captured hidden protein characteristics such as amino acid neighbor interaction and protein secondary structure.
claims.source: Protein profile prediction without sequence alignment was undertaken by Behjati et al., 2022, who proposed a method for single protein profile prediction using the ProtAlbert (Elnaggar et al., 2020b) Transformer. Their work found that attention heads of the pre-trained Transformer captured hidden protein characteristics in the sequence, such as amino acid neighbour interaction, biochemical and biophysical amino acid properties, protein secondary structure, etc.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Behjati et al., 2022 and Elnaggar et al., 2020b.

claims.claim: Mutations in proteins introduce diversity to protein sequences and can either be advantageous in evolution or cause illnesses.
claims.source: Mutations in proteins is another important prediction task. Mutations are a vital part in evolution and introduce diversity to protein sequences. They can either be advantageous in evolution or cause illnesses, for example, a change in a protein's stability may cause a disease.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge in biology.

claims.claim: Yamaguchi and Saito, 2021 used pre-training and fine-tuning of a Transformer for mutation prediction, showing better accuracy than LSTM-based approaches.
claims.source: The approach of pre-training and fine-tuning a Transformer network was undertaken by Yamaguchi and Saito, 2021 for mutation prediction after fine-tuning of the evolutionary information which showed better accuracy compared to using an LSTM-based approach, and by Jiang et al., 2021 to predict the pathogenic missense mutations after pre-training a Transformer and fine-tuning on paired protein sequences which outperformed a variety of existing tools.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Yamaguchi and Saito, 2021 and Jiang et al., 2021.

claims.claim: Jiang et al., 2021 predicted pathogenic missense mutations using a pre-trained and fine-tuned Transformer, outperforming existing tools.
claims.source: The approach of pre-training and fine-tuning a Transformer network was undertaken by Yamaguchi and Saito, 2021 for mutation prediction after fine-tuning of the evolutionary information which showed better accuracy compared to using an LSTM-based approach, and by Jiang et al., 2021 to predict the pathogenic missense mutations after pre-training a Transformer and fine-tuning on paired protein sequences which outperformed a variety of existing tools.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Jiang et al., 2021.

claims.claim: Identifying protein-protein interactions is crucial for understanding protein function in cellular context and for developing therapeutic procedures.
claims.source: To gain insights regarding the function of a protein in its cellular context or to develop therapeutic procedures, it is crucial to identify potential interacting molecules (McDowall et al., 2009; Dick and Green, 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to McDowall et al., 2009 and Dick and Green, 2018.

claims.claim: Identifying drug-target interactions is essential for drug discovery, repurposing existing drugs, and identifying novel protein targets for approved drugs.
claims.source: Similarly, identifying DTI is an essential task that is critical in drug discovery. DTI prediction can contribute by narrowing the search space and prune pairs that are unlikely to bind. The field has expanded to encompass new drug discovery, repurpose drugs already in existence, and identify novel proteins that might be interaction partners for approved drugs (Öztürk et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Öztürk et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Nambiar et al., 2020 used a pre-trained and fine-tuned Transformer for PPI prediction, surpassing results of previously used CNN models.
claims.source: PPI was one of the tasks considered by Nambiar et al., 2020, where a Transformer model was pre-trained and fine-tuned using the HIPPIE database (Alanis-Lobato et al., 2016) they formulated it as a binary classification problem. The method surpassed the results of previously used CNN models.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Nambiar et al., 2020 and Alanis-Lobato et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Lanchantin et al., 2021 predicted human and novel protein interactions through multiple Transformer pre-training stages and fine-tuning on virus-host PPI data, outperforming state-of-the-art methods.
claims.source: Lanchantin et al., 2021 proposed to predict human and novel protein interactions through multiple Transformer pre-training stages (firstly: MLM; secondly: secondary structure, contact, and remote homology prediction) and fine-tuned on virus–host PPI data (Ammari et al., 2016) for binary classification. Their approach outperformed the state-of-the-art method for this task.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Lanchantin et al., 2021 and Ammari et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Xue et al., 2022 carried out cross-species PPI by pre-training a Transformer using sequence, structure, and function features, with embeddings surpassing BiLSTM-only performance.
claims.source: Xue et al., 2022 carried out cross-species PPI by pre-training a Transformer model using three separate features of proteins: sequence, structure, and function. The obtained embedding in combination with embedding from a BiLSTM model surpassed the performance when only the BiLSTM embedding was used.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Xue et al., 2022.

claims.claim: Cai et al., 2021 proposed a new protein embedding through Transformer pre-training that incorporated evolutionary information and outperformed state-of-the-art for DTI prediction.
claims.source: For the DTI prediction, Cai et al., 2021 proposed a new protein embedding through Transformer pre-training that incorporated evolutionary information and used the model's embeddings with a multilayer perceptron trained on several datasets (Gaulton et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2002; Chan et al., 2015; Wishart et al., 2006) to predict chemical-protein binding. The method outperformed the state of the art, which was also based on a Transformer model.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Cai et al., 2021, Gaulton et al., 2012, Chen et al., 2002, Chan et al., 2015, and Wishart et al., 2006.

claims.claim: Wang et al., 2021 predicted drug-target affinity using a pre-trained Transformer with CNN feature extraction, proving more accurate than state-of-the-art DL methods.
claims.source: A method was proposed by wang et al., 2021 to predict drug-target affinity using a regression approach by pre-training a Transformer model and using a CNN to extract features from the learned representation. They utilized multiple datasets (Tang et al., 2014; Davis et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2007) to evaluate their method. The approach proved to be more accurate than the state-of-the-art DL methods, which included a CNN model based on amino acid features and an RNN model based on protein structural features.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to wang et al., 2021, Tang et al., 2014, Davis et al., 2011, and Liu et al., 2007.

claims.claim: PTM is a process of covalent and enzymatic modification of proteins after they are synthesized.
claims.source: PTM is a process of covalent and enzymatic modification of proteins after they are synthesized (Chou, 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Chou, 2020 and is established knowledge.

claims.claim: PTMs provide structural and functional diversity to proteins and are associated with major diseases like cancer.
claims.source: PTMs provide structural and functional diversity to proteins; however, they are also associated with major diseases like cancer.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge in molecular biology.

claims.claim: Qiao et al., 2022 predicted lysine crotonylation using a BiLSTM network trained on BERT embeddings, outperforming state-of-the-art CNN-based models.
claims.source: Prediction of lysine crotonylation, a PTM known to cause diseases like colon cancer and acute kidney injury, was undertaken by Qiao et al., 2022, where a BiLSTM network was trained on BERT (Devlin et al., 2018) embeddings of the amino acids in the protein sequences. The method outperformed the state-of-the-art model based on a CNN that utilised sequence, physicochemical properties, and Word2Vec (Mikolov et al., 2013b) features.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Qiao et al., 2022, Devlin et al., 2018, and Mikolov et al., 2013b.

claims.claim: Zhao et al., 2021 predicted S-nitrosylation using representations from a pre-trained BiLSTM and BERT model, surpassing several state-of-the-art methods.
claims.source: Zhao et al., 2021 attempted to predict S-nitrosylation, a PTM that causes disorders of the cardiovascular, musculoskeletal, and nervous systems. They used representations from a pre-trained BiLSTM model and the representation from a BERT model (Devlin et al., 2018) to encode amino acids. Their approach surpassed the performance of several state-of-the-art methods, including a DL approach that had used position-specific scoring matrices (Jones, 1999) (features from MSA).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Zhao et al., 2021, Devlin et al., 2018, and Jones, 1999.

claims.claim: Wang et al., 2020 predicted several PTMs including phosphorylation by including convolution layers with attention, performing better than existing methods for almost all PTMs.
claims.source: The advantage of attention mechanism is also explored in the work by Wang et al., 2020. In this work, the authors predict several PTMs, including a PTM called phosphorylation, which is one of the most studied PTMs, by including convolution layers with attention. Their framework performed better than existing methods for almost all PTMs.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2020.

claims.claim: Transformer models offer possibilities for visualization and interpretation of their attention weights.
claims.source: Apart from the ground-breaking performance of Transformer models, they also offer possibilities for visualization and interpretation of their attention weights.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about Transformer interpretability.

claims.claim: Analysis of attention heads reveals weight assignments between pairs of input tokens, which can be used to draw conclusions about interactions that contributed to a model's decision.
claims.source: The analysis of attention heads reveal the weight assignments between pairs of input tokens, and these weights can be used to draw conclusions about the interactions between tokens that contributed to a model's decision (Hao et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Hao et al., 2021.

claims.claim: Attention analysis does not necessarily point out feature importance in the representation of the Transformer.
claims.source: Note, however, that such an analysis does not necessarily point out the feature importance in the representation of the Transformer.

It was observed that the fine-tuned model's maps resembled that of contact maps and this pattern was absent from the map prior to fine-tuning. The visualization indicated that the structural information was captured by the model after fine-tuning on evolutionary related sequences.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Yamaguchi and Saito, 2021.

results.result: Transformer-based deep learning models from NLP have led to breakthrough improvements in protein property prediction, overcoming limitations of previous methods and producing state-of-the-art results across diverse tasks.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C11-C14, C66-C67, C100, C158, C185-C186 collectively establish that Transformer models have achieved significant advances in protein prediction tasks. This is supported by multiple citations throughout the review documenting improved performance across structure prediction, homology detection, PTM prediction, and other applications, along with the proof-of-principle experiment (C154-C157) demonstrating superior performance of Transformer features.

results.result: The Transformer model, introduced by Vaswani et al. in 2017, is an encoder-decoder architecture that uses attention mechanisms instead of recurrent or convolutional layers, achieving state-of-the-art language translation results with reduced training time.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C57 describe the original Transformer architecture and its performance, all supported by citation to Vaswani et al., 2017. The architectural details (encoder-decoder structure, attention mechanism, multihead attention with 8 heads, 6 layers, 512-dimensional embeddings) are accurately reported from the original paper.

results.result: Transformer models are trained using self-supervised learning approaches, primarily autoregressive language modeling or masked language modeling (MLM), with MLM becoming particularly popular because it allows models to consider the entire input sequence bidirectionally.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C60 and C46-C48 describe the training approaches for Transformers, supported by multiple citations (Peters et al., 2018; Devlin et al., 2018; Nambiar et al., 2020; Elnaggar et al., 2020a; Rives et al., 2021; and others). The specific detail that typically 15% of tokens are masked in MLM (C59) is supported by citation to Devlin et al., 2018.

results.result: The BERT model, an encoder-only Transformer trained with masked language modeling, achieved state-of-the-art results on 11 NLP tasks and demonstrated that bidirectional pre-training is important for language representations, with larger model size (BERTLARGE) outperforming smaller variants (BERTBASE).
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C65 describe BERT's architecture and performance, all supported by citations to the original BERT paper (Devlin et al., 2018) and related work. The specific architectural details (12 vs 24 layers, 768 vs 1024 dimensions) and performance claims (11 NLP tasks, importance of bidirectional pre-training) are accurately reported from the cited literature.

results.result: Transformer models overcome key limitations of RNNs and CNNs for sequence modeling: RNNs suffer from vanishing/exploding gradients and cannot capture long-range dependencies or parallelize computations, while CNNs require many hierarchical levels to capture distant features and don't utilize positional information. Transformers address these issues through attention mechanisms that directly connect all tokens, enabling parallelization and superior performance.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C79 describe limitations of RNNs and CNNs and advantages of Transformers, all supported by multiple citations (Bengio et al., 1994; Pascanu et al., 2013; Hanin, 2018; Dai et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2019; Raghu et al., 2021; Albawi et al., 2017; Dehghani et al., 2018; Väth et al., 2022). The technical details about gradient problems, parallelization constraints, and attention mechanisms are well-established in the cited literature.

results.result: NLP models can be adapted as protein language models by treating amino acids as tokens and protein sequences as sentences. Despite differences in syntax and semantics, protein sequences contain long-range dependencies suitable for Transformer analysis. These models are trained on large protein databases using self-supervised learning and applied to downstream tasks via feature-based or fine-tuning approaches.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C84, C90-C94 describe the adaptation of NLP models to proteins, supported by citations to Heinzinger et al., 2019; Ofer et al., 2021; Lopez and Mohiuddin, 2020; Ferruz et al., 2022; ElAbd et al., 2020; and Laskar et al., 2020. The conceptual framework for treating proteins as language and the two main application approaches (feature-based and fine-tuning) are well-established in the cited literature.

results.result: The largest open sources of protein sequence data are UniProt (0.567M reviewed + 230M automatically annotated sequences), Pfam (19,632 families, 61M sequences), and BFD (65.9M families, >2B sequences clustered at 30% identity).
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C89 provide specific quantitative data about protein databases, supported by citations to UniProt, 2021; Mistry et al., 2021; Pfam 35.0, 2021; BFD, 2022; and Steinegger et al., 2019. The numerical values are presented as factual data from these cited sources.

results.result: Traditional MSA-based approaches using PSI-BLAST and HMMER have limitations including gaps from insertions/deletions, poor performance for sequences with few homologs, time-consuming database searches, and reliance on imperfect structural features. Protein language models offer advantages by generating embeddings more efficiently and building richer features for low-homology proteins.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C99, C102-C103 describe limitations of MSA-based methods and advantages of protein language models, supported by citations to Altschul et al., 1997; Finn et al., 2011; Golubchik et al., 2007; Phuong et al., 2006; Sułkowska et al., 2012; Schmiedel and Lehner, 2019; Hong et al., 2021; and Wang et al., 2022. The comparative advantages are documented in the cited literature.

results.result: Transformer models have achieved improved performance on protein structure prediction tasks including secondary structure and contact prediction, with studies showing improvements over evolutionary-profile-based methods and state-of-the-art results on CASP benchmarks.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C109 describe specific applications to structure prediction, supported by citations to Rives et al., 2021; Kryshtafovych et al., 2019; Singh et al., 2021; Singh et al., 2022; and Zhang et al., 2021. The performance improvements on CASP benchmarks are documented in the cited studies.

results.result: Transformer-based approaches for homology prediction have shown promise, with methods using ProtAlbert and ProtT5 demonstrating ability to predict protein profiles, detect remote homologs with less preprocessing time than HMMER, and capture hidden protein characteristics including structural hierarchies.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C115 describe applications to homology prediction, supported by citations to Zare-Mirakabad et al., 2021; Elnaggar et al., 2020b; Dodge et al., 1998; Heinzinger et al., 2022; Elnaggar et al., 2020a; Finn et al., 2011; and Behjati et al., 2022. The performance comparisons and capabilities are documented in the cited studies.

results.result: Transformer models have been successfully applied to mutation prediction, with pre-training and fine-tuning approaches showing better accuracy than LSTM-based methods for general mutations and outperforming existing tools for pathogenic missense mutation prediction.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C118 describe applications to mutation prediction, supported by citations to Yamaguchi and Saito, 2021 and Jiang et al., 2021. The performance comparisons are documented in the cited studies.

results.result: Transformer models have demonstrated strong performance on protein-protein interaction (PPI) and drug-target interaction (DTI) prediction tasks, with various approaches outperforming CNN-based, RNN-based, and other state-of-the-art methods across multiple datasets.
results.evaluation: Claims C121-C125 describe applications to interaction prediction, supported by citations to Nambiar et al., 2020; Alanis-Lobato et al., 2016; Lanchantin et al., 2021; Ammari et al., 2016; Xue et al., 2022; Cai et al., 2021; Gaulton et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2002; Chan et al., 2015; Wishart et al., 2006; wang et al., 2021; Tang et al., 2014; Davis et al., 2011; and Liu et al., 2007. The performance improvements are documented in the cited studies.

results.result: Transformer-based approaches have shown superior performance for post-translational modification (PTM) prediction, including lysine crotonylation, S-nitrosylation, and phosphorylation, outperforming CNN-based and other state-of-the-art methods.
results.evaluation: Claims C128-C130 describe applications to PTM prediction, supported by citations to Qiao et al., 2022; Devlin et al., 2018; Mikolov et al., 2013b; Zhao et al., 2021; Jones, 1999; and Wang et al., 2020. The performance comparisons are documented in the cited studies.

results.result: Transformer models offer interpretability through attention weight visualization, allowing analysis of token interactions that contributed to predictions. Studies have shown attention patterns can capture biologically meaningful features like zinc-binding coordination and structural contact maps, though attention weights don't necessarily indicate feature importance.
results.evaluation: Claims C131-C137 describe interpretability of Transformers, supported by citations to Hao et al., 2021; Elnaggar et al., 2020a; Yamaguchi and Saito, 2021; and Zhang et al., 2021, with reference to Figure 5B. The examples of biological insights from attention visualization are documented in the cited studies, and the cautionary note about attention not necessarily indicating feature importance (C133) is appropriate.

results.result: There has been a steady increase in Transformer-related publications since 2017, with 1388 publications found for 'Transformer Language Model' from 2017-2021 in Google Scholar, indicating growing adoption in bioinformatics for studying protein properties.
results.evaluation: Claims C138-C140 present bibliometric data supported by citation to Vaswani et al., 2017 and reference to Figure 6. The specific count of 1388 publications (C139) is presented as data from the authors' Google Scholar search. While the search methodology is straightforward, the interpretation that this indicates effectiveness (C140) is a reasonable inference from the data presented in Figures 6 and 7.

results.result: In a proof-of-principle phosphoglycerylation prediction experiment using 253 samples, Transformer-derived features (ESM-1b and ProtT5) generally outperformed traditional MSA-based features (BigramPGK) and physicochemical features (Phy+Bio) across five classifiers, with concatenated ESM-1b features showing the best overall performance.
results.evaluation: Claims C141-C157 describe the proof-of-principle experiment with detailed methodology and results. The experimental design is clearly described (dataset from Chandra et al., 2019; two Transformer models from Rives et al., 2021 and Elnaggar et al., 2020a; five classifiers; 5-fold CV with 51 held-out test samples). The results in Table 1 support the conclusion that Transformer features generally outperformed traditional features, though the authors appropriately note differences are not always significant (C157).

results.result: Standard Transformer attention mechanisms have limitations including fixed-length input processing and quadratic computational complexity with sequence length. Recent developments address these through techniques like passing hidden states between fragments, sparse attention mechanisms, locality-sensitive hashing, and reversible residual layers.
results.evaluation: Claims C160-C168 describe limitations and solutions, supported by citations to Elnaggar et al., 2020a; Dai et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2019; Zaheer et al., 2020; Kitaev et al., 2020; and Sourkov, 2018. The technical details about computational complexity and proposed solutions are documented in the cited literature.

results.result: Transformers have shown limitations on certain NLP tasks: LSTMs outperformed Transformers on subject-verb agreement and logical inference tasks, Transformers struggled with evaluating logical formulas and modeling hierarchical structures, and GPT-2/GPT-3 had difficulties with poetry and rhyming.
results.evaluation: Claims C169-C172 describe limitations of Transformers, supported by citations to Tran et al., 2018; Hahn, 2020; and Wang et al., 2021. These documented limitations provide important context about tasks where Transformers may not be optimal.

results.result: Larger Transformer models generally achieve better performance but face memory and training time limitations. Solutions include parameter reduction through embedding projection and sharing (Lan et al., 2019), combining autoregressive and bidirectional approaches to address MLM's neglect of masked token dependencies (Yang et al., 2019), and replaced token detection for more efficient learning (Clark et al., 2020).
results.evaluation: Claims C173-C179 describe scaling challenges and solutions, supported by citations to Lan et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2019; Wettig et al., 2022; and Clark et al., 2020. The technical approaches to addressing limitations are documented in the cited literature.

results.result: There is a trend toward building increasingly large Transformer models in NLP (GPT-3 with 175B parameters, Megatron-Turing with 530B, and models exceeding 1 trillion parameters), but this trend may be unsustainable due to resource requirements and could limit protein research to well-funded institutions.
results.evaluation: Claims C182-C184 describe a trend supported by citations (Brown et al., 2020; Smith et al., 2022; Fedus et al., 2021; Narayanan et al., 2021), but the predictions about sustainability (C183) and impact on protein research (C184) are speculative (evidence_type: SPECULATION, INFERENCE). While the concern is reasonable, there is no empirical evidence provided to support these predictions about future trends and their consequences.

results.result: The authors conclude that while Transformers show great promise, they may not be optimal for all protein tasks, other factors beyond architecture may contribute to improvements, hybrid approaches combining Transformers with traditional methods may be beneficial, and the field will likely rely heavily on Transformer-based models in the foreseeable future.
results.evaluation: Claims C189-C190, C195-C197 are primarily speculative conclusions (evidence_type: SPECULATION, INFERENCE) about future directions. While C191-C192 provide supporting examples (MLM with CNNs from Yang et al., 2022; AlphaFold's use of attention), the broader predictions about what approaches will be needed and how the field will develop lack empirical support. These are reasonable perspectives but represent the authors' opinions rather than demonstrated results.

results.result: Protein properties can be global or local, and determining them experimentally is challenging, time-consuming, and costly. There is exponential growth in sequenced proteins but a widening gap with annotated properties, driving interest in computational methods that can provide ranked predictions to guide experimental work.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C10 establish the motivation for computational protein prediction, supported by citations to Walls and Loughran, 2017; Pan et al., 2022; Ehrenberger et al., 2015; UniProt Consortium, 2019; and Varadi et al., 2022. These are well-established facts about the protein annotation gap and the value of computational approaches.

results.result: Machine learning, particularly deep learning, uses neural networks to automatically learn rich feature representations from unstructured data in an end-to-end manner, achieving unprecedented accuracy compared to traditional ML approaches that rely on analyst-determined features.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C26 provide background on ML and DL, supported by citation to Khan et al., 2019 for the claim about unprecedented accuracy (C25). The other claims describe established knowledge about ML/DL concepts (evidence_type: KNOWLEDGE). These are accurate characterizations of the field.

results.result: Common neural network architectures include MLPs (fully connected layers), CNNs (convolution operations for feature detection), and RNNs (sequential processing with recurrent connections including LSTM and GRU variants). RNNs were preferred for NLP tasks for a long time due to their ability to model contextual dependencies.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C37 describe neural network architectures, supported by citations to Koumakis, 2020; Liu et al., 2020; Mikolov et al., 2013a; Zeng et al., 2016; Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997; Chung et al., 2014; Huang et al., 2015; and Yin et al., 2017, with reference to Figure 2. These are accurate descriptions of established architectures.

results.result: NLP evolved from rule-based systems in the 1950s that produced unsatisfactory results to modern DL-based systems that automatically learn from large text datasets. Text is preprocessed through tokenization and converted to numerical embeddings, with DL methods extracting meaningful information more efficiently and accurately than manual feature engineering or human experts.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C45 provide NLP background, supported by citations to Wang et al., 2018; Levy and Goldberg, 2014; Turian and Ratinov, 2010; Young et al., 2018; and Nauman et al., 2019, with reference to Figure 3A. These accurately describe the evolution and current state of NLP.

results.result: Post-translational modifications (PTMs) are covalent enzymatic modifications of proteins after synthesis that change protein functionality, are associated with regulatory cascades and cellular signaling, provide structural and functional diversity, and are associated with diseases like cancer.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C16, C126-C127 describe PTMs, supported by citation to Chou, 2020. These are accurate characterizations of PTMs based on established knowledge in molecular biology.
